issues.title: Private setlist contents remain anonymously readable through the affected RSC and ordinary collection APIs
issues.evidence: For a stored setlist with isPublic:false and an anonymous user, custom GET explicitly returns 403. The RSC page fetches the same slug with trusted Local API semantics and, whenever a document exists, builds and returns title, description, playlist identifiers/URL, track notes and contributor display names without checking isPublic or staff authorization. No ancestor site-layout guard supplies that document policy; public proxy mode passes requests through. Separately, Setlists.access.read unconditionally returns true, allowing ordinary REST/GraphQL document reads irrespective of isPublic, contrary to the field description that unchecked makes the setlist unqueryable and hidden. The owner credential is removed by S1, but the existing private-document boundary itself is bypassable. Current tests assert private rejection only on custom GET and exercise the RSC with isPublic:true.
issues.impact: Anyone who knows/queries a private slug can read a setlist explicitly designated private, including attendee-facing contributed content. This is a concrete authorization inconsistency on the exact browser-bound source under review, not a request for a new music feature or proof of a live incident.
issues.required_action: Custodian should scope the smallest authorization remediation: enforce the existing private visibility rule before RSC serialization and in ordinary collection read filters (retain public documents for ordinary actors and existing verified staff exception), account for relationship population, and add anonymous/customer/staff/private RSC and ordinary-access regressions. Do not solve by granting privileges or denying all public setlists. If source changes, revalidate affected checks and both fresh final reviewers as the packet requires.
